archetype.name: Gunslinger (pocket-holding)
archetype.definition: A quarterback who stays in the pocket hunting intermediate and downfield throws, accepting sacks and turnovers as the price of the big ones, and who this year is playing inside a run-first offense built around an elite defense.

report.headline: Accuracy intact, drives dying on sacks, fumbles and empty short throws
report.take:
Mayfield has always been a high-variance passer: a 2024 peak of 0.207 EPA per play and 41 touchdowns, a slide to 0.089 in 2025, and ints totals that ranked near the bottom of the league almost every year. This season has been a wreck by the topline: -0.271 EPA per dropback, 44th of 49, with a 2.1% touchdown rate that ranks 42nd. The setting matters. Jalon Daniels started weeks 4 through 6, and the dossier doesn't say why. Tampa passes 7.5 points less often than situation predicts (29th), and it leans on a defense ranked 2nd in EPA. Mayfield isn't being asked to carry this team, and when he plays he is often just trying not to lose games the defense is winning.

The accuracy hasn't gone anywhere. His CPOE of +0.28 sits a point above the league average, and his bad-throw rate is down from last year. What is sinking him is everything around the throw. He has taken sacks on 11.3% of dropbacks, and 43.8% of his pressures turn into sacks, 40th of 42. Fifteen of his 18 sacks came in one-score game states, where his EPA per play is -0.576. On third down he is at -0.416 with 8 sacks and a 27.5% conversion rate, though the offense is leaving him an average of 8.6 yards to go. Add three lost fumbles, all in the opener, and the per-dropback number reads as a turnover-and-sack problem more than a passing problem.

The splits show the real shape. His short game is the drain: throws under 10 air yards are completing at 73% yet sit at -0.227 EPA, with 3 of his 4 interceptions on 0-9 yard throws and screens behind the line at -0.209. Once he pushes past 10 yards the plays turn positive (+0.142), and the middle of the field has been his best area at +0.44 on a small sample. He has been efficient under center (72.4% completions, +10.7 CPOE) and poor from shotgun (-0.338), which fits an offense that works when it stays on schedule and falls apart in obvious passing downs. Chris Godwin Jr. (+0.282 per target) and Emeka Egbuka have produced, while targets to Cade Otton (-0.307) and Ted Hurst III (-0.355) have been dead ends. The good numbers when trailing by 9 or more come against soft coverage and shouldn't be trusted. The recent volume collapse is game script: 64 yards in a 43-13 rout, and 0/3 passing in a 16-0 shutout win.

Going forward, some of this should correct. A 2.1% touchdown rate is far below anything in his career, and fumble losses at this rate rarely hold. The sack habit is partly who he is. His pressure-to-sack rate has been in the high 30s for three straight years, so expect improvement toward that level, not a cure. The ceiling on volume is structural. This is a run-first team with a top-two defense, so even a healthier Mayfield looks like a 200-yard passer most weeks, with spikes only when an opponent forces a shootout.

strengths.title: Ball placement still holds up
strengths.body: His completion percentage over expected is above the league average, and his bad-throw rate improved from last season even as the results cratered. That points away from a decline in arm or touch and toward the sacks and fumbles around the throw. Accuracy that has held up across his career should stay.

strengths.title: Intermediate and middle throws produce
strengths.body: When he gets the ball 10+ yards downfield, and especially between the numbers, the plays add value. That has been his game for years as an aggressive pocket passer. The samples are modest (35 intermediate attempts, 22 to the middle), but the throws he is built to make are the ones working.

strengths.title: On-schedule, under-center efficiency
strengths.body: From under center he completes 72.4% with a big positive CPOE and a near-neutral EPA, while shotgun dropbacks have been a disaster. With a top-10 rushing offense, staying ahead of the chains and using play-action looks is the sustainable path for him.

concerns.title: Sacks swallowing close-game drives
concerns.body: An 11.3% sack rate and a 43.8% pressure-to-sack rate are the single biggest drag on his EPA, and they pile up in one-score games and on third down. Part of this is career-long, a pocket gunslinger holding the ball to hunt downfield, and his time to throw is up from last year. It is worse than his norm, though, so some regression is due, but not a full fix.

concerns.title: Turnovers on low-value throws
concerns.body: Three of his four interceptions came on 0-9 yard throws, which drags the short game negative despite a high completion rate. He also has six turnover-worthy fumbles. The three lost fumbles all came in week 1, which looks more like a bad afternoon than a trend, but the short-area interceptions are a decision-making issue worth watching.

concerns.title: Volume capped by team identity
concerns.body: Tampa is among the most run-leaning teams relative to situation, and with an elite defense it can win games where he throws 11 or 3 passes. That's a product of his role, not a flaw, but it keeps his passing yardage and touchdown ceiling low in any game the Bucs control.

trend.note: Three hard-luck starts to open the year, a three-week absence, then a stretch where game script all but removed him (64 yards, then 0/3) before a 32-attempt, two-interception game at Chicago. The efficiency has barely moved; only the volume swings with the score.

nextGame.headline: A leaky Detroit secondary, but a pass rush built to sack him
nextGame.body:
Detroit is the best passing matchup he has seen. It ranks 27th against the pass, gives up the most fantasy points and passing yards to quarterbacks, and is soft both short (28th) and deep. It is also the 2nd-strongest pass funnel in the league, and its own offense is 4th in pass EPA, so this sets up as the kind of game that forces Tampa off its run-first script. The catch is the pass rush: Detroit is 5th in hit rate and 7th in sack rate, aimed squarely at his biggest weakness. It's a dome game with two weeks of rest behind him after the bye.

Availability tilts his way. Linebacker Jack Campbell, a 97%-snap player, is on injured reserve until at least early December, which thins the middle of the field where Mayfield does his best work and where tight ends have feasted on Detroit. Cornerback D.J. Reed (94% of snaps) and linebacker DJ Wonnum were ruled out last week with estimated returns before this game, so check their status. Reed back would tighten the outside, and safety Kerby Joseph hasn't played this season. On Tampa's side, Mayfield practiced fully, and Jalen McMillan's IR stint barely matters given his 7% snap share. No line is posted yet.

keyMatchups.title: Detroit's rush vs his sack habit
keyMatchups.body: Detroit gets home often, and Mayfield converts pressure into sacks at one of the worst rates in the league. If he gets the ball out, the coverage behind that rush is beatable. If he holds it, this game looks like his one-score splits.

keyMatchups.title: Middle of field without Campbell
keyMatchups.body: Detroit has allowed tight ends far over their averages, and losing its every-down linebacker makes the seams and intermediate middle even softer. That is Mayfield's most productive area, and it could finally make Otton a positive target instead of a drain.

keyMatchups.title: Shootout pressure on script
keyMatchups.body: Detroit's passing offense ranks near the top, and opponents throw on it far more than usual. That should push Tampa into more dropbacks than its run-first norm, raising his volume. It also exposes him to more obvious passing downs, where he has struggled.

nextGame.watch: How quickly he gets rid of the ball on early downs. If the sack count stays at two or fewer, the matchup should pay off.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect better efficiency than he has shown, without a return to 2024. His accuracy is intact and his touchdown rate is unsustainably low for a passer with his history, so touchdowns should come more often. The lost fumbles were concentrated in one game, and a pressure-to-sack rate this far above even his own elevated career norm should ease. What won't change is the structure. A run-first offense paired with a top-two defense means many games where he throws in the low 20s, so a reasonable range is roughly 165-225 passing yards and about one touchdown a game, with shootout matchups like Detroit as the upside weeks.

The sack rate is the lever. If it settles near his recent-career levels, his EPA climbs toward roughly average and the offense's third-down issues ease. If it stays here, he remains a bottom-tier efficiency passer regardless of the touchdown luck. Godwin and Egbuka getting the bulk of the targets over Otton and Hurst would also help.
swingFactors: Game scripts that force Tampa to pass
Target share shifting to Godwin and Egbuka

confidence.note: Six starts with a mid-season absence, two of them near-zero volume; career baseline supports regression.
